title: The hidden history behind Tūmatauenga
description: A scholarly look at Tūmatauenga: etymology, pronunciation, and the fight to keep original names on the web.
author: PuniCodex Team
body:
# The hidden history behind Tūmatauenga

Behind the modern ASCII form *tumatauenga* hides a much longer story. ​**Tūmatauenga** reaches back through manuscripts, inscriptions, and oral tradition long before it ever touched a keyboard, and every mark in the restored spelling is a receipt from that journey. In what follows we trace ‌the name from its Polynesian transcription attestations through its mythology, its cult, its symbols, and its afterlife in other cultures — and we show how the PuniCodex project turned that philological record into ‌a Unicode domain that resolves today. The history was never lost. It was only waiting for the infrastructure to catch up.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Tūmatauenga
- **ASCII form:** tumatauenga
- **Meaning:** "'The man of ​furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind"
- **Domain of influence:** War, Humanity, Strength
- **Pantheon:** Polynesian
- **Restoration:** Preserves vowel length
- **Live domain:** tūmatauenga.com

## Overview

**Tūmatauenga** (*tumatauenga*) — The ​Face of Battle — belongs to the Polynesian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "War, Humanity, Strength". The name means "'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god ​of war and of humankind".

Tūmatauenga is the Māori god of war and of humanity's fierce inheritance: the one son of the Sky Father who stood firm when the storm-god attacked, and who then ​subdued his own brothers — taking their fishes, their birds, and their crops — to feed the people he had made. War, in his story, is the price of standing.

PuniCodex restores the ​name as **Tūmatauenga** and serves its temple at [tūmatauenga.com](https://xn--tmatauenga-5dc.com). The restoration preserves a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the macron on ū marking the long vowel —. The plain ASCII form *tumatauenga* ‌survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for ​this name; **Tūmatauenga** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind".

The ASCII ​form *tumatauenga* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Tūmatauenga** recovers the vowel length of the original ‌directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the macron on ū marking the long vowel —.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **t** → **T** — Same ​letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **m** → **m** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter
- **t** → **t** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same ‌letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **e** → **e** — Same letter
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **g** → **g** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter

The project holds ​the domain **tūmatauenga.com** (xn--tmatauenga-5dc.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual polynesian names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.

‌The form **Tūmatauenga** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

Te ​reo Māori writes him with the macron as the vowel-length it is: Tūmatauenga. The oral text is the truer scripture — the whakataukī "Ka mate kāinga tahi, ka ora kāinga rua" and the karakia ​of war and planting carry his name in the living language, and the New Zealand Army's Māori name, Ngāti Tūmatauenga, writes it into the state itself.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name ​is **/tuː.ma.taʊ.ˈe.ŋa/** — Māori.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: TOO-mah-tow-ENG-ah, long ū on the first syllable.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Māori** — Tūmatauenga
- **Hawaiian twin** — Kū
- **NZ ​Army** — Ngāti Tūmatauenga
- **Owned form** — Tūmatauenga

Tūmatauenga is pronounced with the long ū of the first syllable — the macron the restoration keeps — and the name means "Tū of the ​angry face": tū (to stand, and the god's name) plus mata (face) plus anga (the -ing of appearance). He is the Māori war-god, and his name is a face set for war.

## Mythology

Tūmatauenga's ‌cycle is the Polynesian account of how humanity got its arts: not by gift but by conquest — the war-god subduing his elemental brothers and distributing the spoils to his mortal children.

### The ​Sons of Rangi and Papa (The Separation)

In the beginning the Sky Father (Ranginui) and the Earth Mother (Papatūānuku) lay locked together, and their sons lived crushed in darkness between them. Tūmatauenga, fiercest of ‌the brothers, urged that the parents be killed; the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed — they would be forced apart. Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tāne each tried and failed to push them; then ​Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore the parents open. Light came into the world — and war came with it.

### The One Who Stood (The Storm)

‌Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation, and now he attacked his brothers in revenge: Tangaroa fled to the sea, the gods of food hid in the earth and the ​forest — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast against the storm, unbowed on the open plain. When the tempest spent itself, the war-god turned on his fleeing brothers: he made nets and took Tangaroa's ‌fish, snared Tāne's birds, and dug up Rongo's and Haumia's crops. His standing made humanity heir to every domain.

### The Arts of War and Peace (The Inheritance)

By subduing his brothers, Tūmatauenga made their ​realms noa — common, usable — and so gave humankind its technologies: net and hook for the sea, snare for the forest, the digging-stick for the garden. The karakia of planting, fishing, and ‌war all carry his name; the Māori tradition is explicit that the fierce god is also the culture-bringer. His children — humanity, in the southern traditions — inherited both the standing and the storm.

### ​The Sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku (The Separation)

In the beginning the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked together in an embrace, and their children lived crushed in darkness ​between them. Among the sons was **Tūmatauenga**, fiercest of them all. When the brothers debated what to do, it was Tū who urged the final solution — kill the parents and have done. The ‌others recoiled at the thought of slaying their own father and mother, and the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed: the parents would be forced apart, not slain (Grey, *Polynesian Mythology*, the legend of ‌the children of Rangi and Papa). Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tū himself tried to push the parents and failed; then Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore ‌the parents open. Light came into the world — and Tāwhirimātea, who had loved the darkness, went to war over it. The myth is exact about its genealogy of war: strife is not ​an intruder into creation but a sibling of the light itself, born the moment separation was chosen.

### The Arts Won by Conquest (The Spoils)

By subduing his brothers, Tūmatauenga made their realms *noa* — ​common, usable — and so gave humankind its technologies: the net and hook for the sea, the snare for the forest, the digging-stick for the garden. The karakia of planting, fishing, fowling, and ‌war all carry his name, for every tapu those arts break was broken first by him; Best and Tregear record his invocation where food is made safe to eat. The cycle thus makes ​the fiercest god the culture-bringer: not Tāne the gentle separator but Tū the stander, who gathered what the storm scattered and portioned it out. The distribution is the myth's second doctrine. What war wins ​must be handed on; the conqueror who keeps everything for himself defeats the purpose of standing, and the tribe that forgets how to feed itself has lost the spoils twice.

### The Children of ‌Tū (The Descent)

The tradition gives the war-god a family larger than any brotherhood: humankind itself. Tregear records the phrase *he tamaiti nā Tū* — 'a child of Tū' — as a way of ​naming a human being (*The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary*, s.v. Tu), and the southern branches of the family tell the same descent as genealogy: in Tahiti, Tū is not only the war-god but the ​first ancestor, the root of the human line (Henry, *Ancient Tahiti*). The Māori cycles draw the moral plainly. The brothers who fled or hid left their domains to be taken; the one who stood ‌gave humans his own nature — fierceness, endurance, and the habit of war. To be human, in this theology, is to have inherited the furious face; the arts of peace, Rongo's garden and ​Tangaroa's sea, are the domains of humankind's gentler uncles, conquered and kept only because their fierce brother stands guard over them.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Tūmatauenga concentrates in a small set ‌of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The taiaha** — The long staff-weapon of chiefly combat — spear and club in one lineage
- **The haka** — The war-dance: the body ​made into the angry face of the god
- **The feather cloak** — The kahu huruhuru of the war-chief — honour worn on the shoulders

- **The pūkana** — The widened eyes and out-thrust tongue of ​the war-face — the literal mata of his name, worn by every performer

## Archaeology & Evidence

New Zealand's ridgelines keep his monuments: thousands of pa — terraced, ditched, and palisaded hill-forts — from ​the classic period, with sites like Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill) among the largest earthworks of the Pacific. The greenstone mere and the carved taiaha of the museum collections (Te Papa's among them) are ​his regalia; the Auckland War Memorial Museum — itself a cenotaph to the fallen — houses the war-canoes and the martial taonga of his people. The kumara storage-pits beside every pa tie his war-and-garden ‌cycle into the ground itself.

## Realm & Domain

Tūmatauenga is the Māori god of war and of humanity's fierce inheritance: the one son of the Sky Father who stood firm when the storm-god ‌attacked, and who then subdued his own brothers — taking their fishes, their birds, and their crops — to feed the people he had made. War, in his story, is the price of standing.

### ​The Mere

The flat greenstone club of the chief — the weapon that is also a badge of rank and a gift of state.

### The Angry Face

His name: the war-face (pūkana) that ‌the haka still performs with widened eyes and out-thrust tongue.

### The Nets and Hooks

He snared his brother Tangaroa's fish: the arts of fishing, won by war and given to man.

### The Pa

The ​fortified hill-settlement — his architecture, crowning New Zealand's ridgelines by the thousand.

## Across Cultures

He is one face of a Polynesian-wide god: Hawaiian Kū — the great war-god of the feathered helmets and ​the luakini temples — Tahitian Tū, and the Cook Islands' war deities share his name and his office, the deepest layer of pan-Polynesian religion. In New Zealand his worship ran through the war-parties and ‌their tohunga; the 19th-century Māori military genius (the gunfighter pa of the New Zealand Wars) applied his standing to musket and trench, and the New Zealand Army today bears his name as its ‌own: Ngāti Tūmatauenga, "the tribe of the war-god."

Within the Polynesian tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[kanaloa|Kānāloa]], [[papatuanuku|Papatūānuku]], [[tane|Tāne]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[anat|ꜥAnat]], and [[ares|Árēs]].

## Cultural Legacy

The haka — performed by the ‌All Blacks before every match and by the army at every farewell — is his face in modern life: the widened eyes and out-thrust tongue are the literal mata anga of his name. ‌Ngāti Tūmatauenga, the army's Māori designation, makes him the only ancient god officially patron of a modern state's armed forces. His cycle — the standing against the storm, the conquest that feeds the ​people — remains the charter myth of Māori resilience, quoted in land-march speeches and waiata alike.

## A Meditation

Tūmatauenga is the god of standing your ground — and of what standing costs. He alone faced the storm, and so he alone could feed the people; but the myth ‌hides nothing: his fierceness proposed killing the parents, and his victories are his brothers' defeats. He asks the hardest question of every defender: what are you standing against — and what, when you ​have won, will your strength feed?

## The Unicode Restoration

Tūmatauenga preserves vowel length. The ASCII fallback *tumatauenga* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the ​11 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 1: 1 mark of length (ū). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Character by Character

The journey from ​*tumatauenga* to **Tūmatauenga**, one character at a time:

- **t** → **T** — Same letter
- **u** → **ū** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **m** → **m** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same ‌letter
- **t** → **t** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **e** → **e** — Same letter
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **g** → ​**g** — Same letter
- **a** → **a** — Same letter

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **tūmatauenga.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--tmatauenga-5dc.com — ​an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Tūmatauenga; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the ​entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Polynesian transcription can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does Tūmatauenga mean?** The traditional gloss is "'The man of furious face' (tū ‌+ mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind."

**Which tradition does Tūmatauenga belong to?** Tūmatauenga is catalogued in the Polynesian pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**What does Tūmatauenga preserve that ASCII cannot ​show?** The form itself answers: Tūmatauenga preserves vowel length — and the marks in the restored spelling are exactly that evidence.

**Is Tūmatauenga a working domain?** Yes — tūmatauenga.com resolves today and routes ‌to this temple.

**What is the punycode for tūmatauenga.com?** The DNS encoding is xn--tmatauenga-5dc.com; browsers perform the translation automatically, so visitors only ever see the restored name.

**Can I use Tūmatauenga in a normal ​browser?** Yes. The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool on this site converts tumatauenga to Tūmatauenga for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry ‌is built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

## Why This Restoration Matters

The story of Tūmatauenga did not end ‌in antiquity; it changed medium. Names that survive for millennia do so because each generation finds a new carrier for them — clay, papyrus, print, and now DNS. The PuniCodex restoration simply makes ​the carrier honest: the spelling that resolves is the spelling the evidence supports. If this post showed anything, it is that *tumatauenga* and **Tūmatauenga** are not the same name with different styling. They ​are a summary and the text it summarizes. The web can now serve the text.
